The Last Safe Detour for Oil Just Took a Drone Hit

Nobody has claimed responsibility for Wednesday's drone strike that set two gas tankers ablaze at Egypt's Damietta port, and nobody needs to, the oil market already knows exactly what it's worth. 

"The passage through the Red Sea, even via the longer Mediterranean route, could be put at risk, which threatens up to five million barrels per day of oil supply that can currently bypass the Strait of Hormuz," said Saul Kavonic of MST Marquee, Reuters reports. 

Hormuz is already effectively closed. Bab el-Mandeb is now half-empty after Houthi threats. Suez and the Sumed pipeline were the last detour left, and someone just put a drone through it.

The scramble is already visible on the water. Roughly 30 ships are now clustered at the Port Said anchorage, up from 20 earlier in the week, and crude moving through Sumed has jumped from 19.5 million barrels in April to nearly 29 million in July. 

"We've seen a clear increase in crude/condensate tankers heading north after loading in the Red Sea," said Vortexa's George Morris, attributing the shift directly to Houthi threats. 

Some vessels are getting explicit Houthi permission to pass Bab el-Mandeb anyway, including Chinese ships, while a growing number are simply switching off their trackers and hoping.

And yet oil prices fell on Thursday, the same day a chokepoint tanker route got hit by an unclaimed drone, because traders were more interested in Iranian-Omani talks over Hormuz. 

"The market isn't pricing in disruption to the canal at this stage," said S&P Global's Aly Blakeway, which is either remarkable discipline or remarkable denial. 

The insurance side isn't nearly as relaxed: "Insurers may also command higher Additional War Risk Premiums for Suez in light of the attack, given the increased risk to shipping and energy infrastructure in the region," warned Argus's Martin Senior. 

Someone is going to profit off this uncertainty either way, it just won't be the tanker crews rerouting around Africa for an extra month of transit time.

So the last working oil corridor in the region just absorbed a drone strike nobody owns, prices dropped anyway, and the only people moving with real urgency are the insurers calculating the premium. Who exactly is pricing this war, the traders watching diplomacy in Oman, or the underwriters watching the drones?

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.
